pages.title: A catalyst changes the route, not the destination

blocks.text: A catalyst can make product appear faster. Does that prove it increases equilibrium yield? A new pathway can speed both directions while preserving their final balance.
A catalyst increases the rate of reaching equilibrium without changing K or equilibrium composition at the same conditions. It cannot make a strongly reactant-favoured equilibrium product-favoured.

pages.transition: Temperature, unlike a catalyst, can alter the final ratio.

pages.title: Temperature affects rate and equilibrium differently

blocks.text: Heating often speeds reactions, but its equilibrium effect depends on enthalpy: it favours the endothermic direction. Reaction rate and equilibrium yield can therefore improve in opposite temperature directions.
Cooling favours ammonia in its exothermic synthesis but lowers the rate. A catalyst helps the rate trade-off. Compare final equilibrated mixtures, rather than product amounts after equal short times.

pages.transition: In water, the particles taking part in equilibrium are often ions.

pages.title: Mobile ions make an electrolyte

blocks.text: Electrolytes supply mobile ions in solution and allow electrical conduction. Strong electrolytes are substantially dissociated or ionised in dilute water. Weak electrolytes establish an equilibrium containing appreciable unionised molecules.
NaCl dissolves as ions, while ethanoic acid reacts with water only partly to form H₃O⁺ and CH₃COO⁻. Molecular sugar solution does not provide the same mobile-ion population.
Dissociation separates pre-existing ions. Ionisation forms ions from a molecular solute through interaction with the solvent.

pages.transition: How much is present differs from how completely it ionises.

pages.title: Strong does not mean concentrated

blocks.text: Concentration measures solute amount per volume. Strength describes the extent of ion formation under specified conditions. A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both possible.

Conductivity also depends on ion concentration and mobility, so the word strong alone does not fix conductivity. Never taste or touch a substance to classify it as acidic or basic; use appropriate indicators or measurements.

pages.transition: The Arrhenius definition identifies the ions produced in water.

pages.title: Arrhenius acids and bases

blocks.text: An Arrhenius acid increases hydrogen-ion concentration in water; an Arrhenius base increases hydroxide-ion concentration. Aqueous protons associate with water and are commonly represented as H₃O⁺.
HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ illustrates an aqueous acid. NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) supplies hydroxide as a base. This framework specifically concerns aqueous behaviour.

pages.transition: A broader definition tracks proton transfer itself.

pages.title: Brønsted–Lowry follows H⁺

blocks.text: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton, H⁺; a Brønsted–Lowry base accepts one. These roles occur together because a donor needs an acceptor.
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₃ accepts H⁺ and is the base. Water donates H⁺ and is the acid. This explains ammonia basicity without requiring OH⁻ in its original formula.

pages.transition: After transfer, each partner has a conjugate form.

pages.title: Conjugate pairs differ by one proton

blocks.text: Removing H⁺ from an acid gives its conjugate base. Adding H⁺ to a base gives its conjugate acid. A pair differs by exactly one H⁺ and one charge unit.
In the ammonia reaction, the pairs are NH₄⁺/NH₃ and H₂O/OH⁻. NH₃ and OH⁻ are not a conjugate pair with each other. Removing H⁺ from HCO₃⁻ gives CO₃²⁻, not CO₃⁻.

pages.transition: The same substance can donate or accept depending on its partner.

pages.title: Water plays both roles

blocks.text: With HCl, water accepts H⁺ and acts as a base. With NH₃, it donates H⁺ and acts as an acid. This ability to show both behaviours is called amphoteric behaviour.
Acid or base is a reaction role, not a label determined merely by containing hydrogen. HCO₃⁻ can also accept or donate H⁺ depending on the reaction partner.
Track the product charge as a check: accepting positive H⁺ raises the charge by one; donating it lowers the charge by one.

pages.transition: Apply proton and charge bookkeeping to a new pair of reactants.

pages.title: Worked conjugate-pair assignment

blocks.text: Teacher-created reaction: HNO₂ + CN⁻ ⇌ NO₂⁻ + HCN. HNO₂ loses H⁺ and is the acid. CN⁻ gains H⁺ and is the base. The conjugate pairs are HNO₂/NO₂⁻ and HCN/CN⁻. Total charge remains −1 on both sides.
Do not alter oxygen counts or central atoms when constructing a conjugate partner. Only one H⁺ is transferred; changing other atoms creates a different species.

pages.transition: Revise the catalyst, electrolyte and acid–base distinctions.

pages.title: Revision: track ions and proton transfer

blocks.text: A catalyst changes the time to equilibrium, while temperature can change K. Electrolyte strength describes ion formation; concentration describes solute amount per volume.

Arrhenius acids and bases increase aqueous hydrogen and hydroxide ions respectively. Brønsted–Lowry acids donate H⁺ and bases accept it. Conjugate partners differ by one proton; amphoteric water can play either role.

questions.question: Does a catalyst change K at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: No. It changes the rate of approach, not the endpoint constant.

questions.question: Can a strong acid be dilute?
questions.answer: Yes. Strength concerns ionisation, while dilute concerns concentration.

questions.question: Why is NH₃ a base with water?
questions.answer: It accepts a proton to become NH₄⁺.

questions.question: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
Are H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ a conjugate pair?
questions.answer: No. They differ by two protons; H₃O⁺/H₂O and H₂O/OH⁻ are pairs.

questions.question: Why can water be both acid and base?
questions.answer: It can accept H⁺ from one partner or donate H⁺ to another.
